prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, enabling frequency measurement at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Having read all eight opening ballots, I have moved from my own first choice to the optical lattice clock. It is the one candidate that nearly everyone ranked (seven of eight ballots, two first places, four top-three placements), and the support comes from members with very different backgrounds, which says more than any single enthusiastic ranking. The invention is clear: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice makes it possible to interrogate many neutral atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime with the light shift cancelled, and Ye's group took the strontium clock to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and many-body-limited operation. It has been reproduced independently at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and elsewhere, it supports relativistic geodesy and tests of fundamental constants, and it is the basis for the planned redefinition of the second. As an experimentalist I value that it is an instrument whose performance is measured against an external standard, not argued over. The two-name credit is clean and avoids the large-collaboration allocation problem that complicates IceCube and the Higgs.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision frequency metrology has already been honoured recently (Hall and Haensch in 2005 for the comb, Wineland in 2012 for ion control), so the committee must be able to state what is new: the neutral-atom many-body lattice and the 1e-18 regime, not clocks in general. The role of the broader optical-clock community (PTB and NIST ion clocks, the Paris lattice work, other groups) also makes the line between inventor and refiner contestable, and the redefinition of the second is still pending, so some will say the prize is slightly ahead of the practical payoff. Finally, I rank IceCube higher on discovery content, and choosing the better-supported candidate over my own field of preference should not be mistaken for a belief that the neutrino case is weaker scientifically.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B006 first and B007 third, and values discovery of new phenomena over improved measurements; he sees the IceCube diffuse flux as a new window on the cosmos, though with allocation difficulty and partial source identification.
responses.response: I agree with the characterisation of IceCube and it is why I opened with it. But the ballots show it has only six rankings, with three of them at seventh or eighth, so it does not have the breadth a prize needs. I also take his point on discovery-centred merit seriously, and that is why I keep B006 and B007 as alternatives. I disagree that a measurement-driven candidate is lesser: the lattice clock is an invention that has opened new observational access to gravitational redshift at millimetre scales and to searches for variation of constants. I would add that his own ranking placed B015 fourth, so the gap between us is smaller than the first-place ballots suggest.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B015 first on the grounds that Katori's magic-wavelength proposal plus Ye's record-accuracy realisation give a clean two-person prize, independently confirmed by many laboratories, and notes that comb and ion-clock work is already recognised.
responses.response: I agree on the two-person attribution and on maturity, and I find his argument about independent confirmation across JILA, RIKEN, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and NPL the most persuasive evidence for timing. Where I would qualify his position is the earlier prizes: the citation should be written tightly around the neutral-atom lattice and the uncertainty regime reached, so that it is not read as a second prize for the comb or for ion clocks. I do not share his sense that this is clearly the winner over the moire case, since my opening placed it only fifth and I want the committee to test the 2005 and 2012 overlap properly.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B015 first, stressing that the lattice clock rests on atomic-structure ideas, reaches 1e-18, and has lasting importance for metrology, geodesy and fundamental-physics searches; she also notes that the SI second redefinition is pending.
responses.response: I agree with her reading of the importance, and her point that agreement across Sr, Yb and other species at 1e-18 shows the result does not depend on a single laboratory carries weight with me. I would press one reservation: she flags that other groups, including the Paris work and the ion-clock community, contributed, and I think we should say explicitly why we credit Katori and Ye over them. I also note that she ranks the Higgs third like me; I do not think the two cases are in competition, but the Higgs attribution problem remains unresolved and is the reason I would not put it in the preferred configuration.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B023 (KPZ universality) first and B015 second, and regards the twisted-graphene discovery as defensible but somewhat early because the pairing mechanism remains debated.
responses.response: I agree with him on B006: the core observations are solid and widely reproduced, but the origin of the superconductivity is not settled, and that makes me prefer the clock now and hold moire matter as an alternative for a later year. On KPZ I cannot add much from my own field; his ballot is the only one that ranks it, so I would need to hear a case for why it should displace candidates with broader backing. His second-place ranking of B015 with a clean two-name credit does support my choice.

uncertainties: How the committee should frame novelty relative to the 2005 (comb) and 2012 (ion control) prizes in a citation for B015.
Whether the contributions of other lattice-clock groups outside the supplied names change the two-person allocation.
Whether the twisted bilayer graphene case will be regarded as settled once the superconducting mechanism is better understood.
Whether the individual weights of Halzen, Karle and Spiering in the IceCube discovery can be fairly established for a prize.
statement.conflict_note: My own research (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur) is in experimental astroparticle physics, so I have a field-adjacent interest in B007 (IceCube) and in the Higgs candidate through my CERN-based doctoral background, and I should recuse myself from or at least disclose that interest when those are weighed. My profile documents no specific tie to IceCube, ATLAS or CMS, or to any candidate in my preferred B015 configuration.
